direct_claims: Child mortality rate is defined as the estimated share of newborns who die before reaching the age of five.
derived_claims: This is a Marimekko chart published by Our World in Data representing global child mortality rates in 2023.
The chart visualizes child mortality rates on the vertical axis and country populations as a share of the global total on the horizontal axis.
The data is sourced from the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (2025).
African nations (colored purple) like Niger and Angola exhibit some of the highest child mortality rates, with Niger exceeding 10%.
Highly populated countries like India and China span large widths on the X-axis, representing their massive shares of the global population.
India's child mortality rate is around 2.8%, while China's is significantly lower, under 1%.

The stark contrast between regions—such as European nations having rates well below 1% (e.g., Belarus at 0.24%) compared to African nations with rates above 5% or 10%—highlights deep global inequalities in healthcare infrastructure and living standards.

The chart groups countries by world regions, showing that Europe and North America generally cluster at the low-mortality, right-hand side of the distribution, while Africa dominates the high-mortality, left-hand side.
speculative_claims: In a Marimekko chart, the area of each bar represents the absolute number of child deaths, as it multiplies the rate (height) by the population size (width).
Child mortality is a key indicator of child health and well-being, reflecting access to basic healthcare, clean water, sanitation, and nutrition.

Policymakers and global health organizations (like UNICEF or WHO) use this data to target interventions and resources to high-burden areas to meet Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) related to child survival.
